messages.subject: cpo and diagonal
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to compare two models with the cpo values.

I am getting some observations with failure==1.

The inla.cpo takes too much time and when the models are more than two then it's endless...
eg for a model that takes 2mins, the inla.cpo needs more than 15mins (without recomputing the mode).

With control.inla(diagonal=value) the number of points with failure==1 are much less (50 out of 4800) than without (280 out of 4800)

So, if both (all) models have diagonal=value, and then the inla.cpo is called, is the comparison of the models still valid?
or... under the proper way (without diagonal=value) I could expect a different model with better cpo/logarithmic score?
any hints in that case to make the cpo calculation faster? or the number of points with failure==1 less?

Best,
Alex

Hi

the diagonal=value is not a good option here, as it change the model. it
make sense that you'll get less failures with increasing values, as you
basically adds an extra prior term that will push the latent field
towards zero.

The question is if make sense to add another option assuming
Gaussianity, to speed up the calculations. This will basically remove
all failures (ie we assume they do not appear...). I'll try to look into
these details.

The benefite will be faster and more approximate cpo values. Of'course
the more accurate way will still be in the code.

I give it a thought and post a more accurate respose here soon.

If anyone has a better idea(s), please let me know.

parts:
On Tue, 2013-07-30 at 04:26 -0700, Aritz Alberdi wrote:
> Hi there,
>
> I would like to ask possibly a stupid question about the failures>0.
>
> what does it essentially mean? what assumptions are violated?
> assumptions for the calculation of CPO and PIT values? or assumptions
> of the fitted model?

The cpo values are computed from the posterior density of the linear
predictor eta[i] without the contribution from the i'th datapoint y[i].
They way that it is computed, assumes that for the posterior density for
eta[i] with all the data and without y[i], does not change to much. If
they have in practice, no the same support, we will get a division by 0
situation. So internally, this is checked for and if the conditions are
ok, then failure=0 and =1 if not. if failure is 1 then the cpo-values
are not compute, and are simply set to 0 (I think). there is a function
'inla.cpo' that can be used to compute the 'failure' ones 'manually'.
There is also a question if we could approximate these in another way
using just Gaussians...

> I mean, if failure>0, this means that our model has some kind of
> problem?
not really, but it says that y[i] has a big impact on eta[i].
